1.name: K'yeon Moore
1.about: The projected No. 1 pick in a weaker draft class, Moore separated himself with one of the most productive freshman seasons in the country. He thrives creating inside the arc, controlling pace and using his strength and craft to consistently reach his spots, while showing enough range and playmaking to command an offense. His combination of production, scoring versatility and advanced feel has made him the safest bet at the top of this class.

2.name: Wu Xin
2.about: One of the premier prospects in the class, Wu has emerged as a legitimate candidate to come off the board near the very top of the draft. His combination of interior scoring, passing feel and developing floor-spacing gives him unusual offensive versatility at center. He can facilitate from multiple areas of the floor, punish mismatches inside and provide value without dominating possessions.

3.name: Kendall Williams
3.about: Williams has firmly worked his way into the conversation as a top-three pick, offering one of the most imposing physical and defensive profiles in the class. The BYU freshman combines elite explosiveness with a 7'2" wingspan, making him a devastating weak-side rim protector, lob threat and offensive rebounder. His developing offensive skill set remains the biggest swing factor in just how high his ceiling can reach.

4.name: Tate Woods
4.about: Arguably possessing the highest ceiling of any prospect in the class, Woods' No. 4 projection is driven more by long-term potential than current production. At 6'10" with a 7'2" wingspan, he flashes advanced midrange touch, intriguing perimeter skill and major defensive upside. His freshman production was inconsistent, but continued physical and offensive development could eventually turn him into a uniquely versatile two-way forward.

5.name: Dashaun Williams
5.about: Few big men in the class can match Williams’ combination of mobility, length and explosive athleticism. The North Carolina freshman thrives attacking the basket, running the floor and creating matchup problems with his movement. His defensive versatility and ability to impact possessions around the rim give him the two-way upside expected from a top-five prospect.

6.name: Nathan Essome
6.about: Once projected as a top-two pick, Essome remains one of the class's most intriguing guard prospects despite sliding slightly down the board. He combines aggressive downhill attacking with impressive passing instincts, creating for teammates off penetration and in transition. His length and athleticism also provide defensive upside, while improving his jumper remains the biggest step toward maximizing his offensive potential.

7.name: Brady Colby
7.about: Widely regarded as the best shooter in the class, Colby backed up that reputation with an impressive freshman season at Duke. His deep range and ability to connect both off movement and off the dribble make him exceptionally difficult to cover. While shooting drives his projection, he is also an underrated defender, using his strong frame, positioning and effort to hold his own across multiple matchups.

8.name: Ishaan Cooper
8.about: One of the class's most explosive wing athletes, Cooper made an immediate impact at Kansas with his ability to overwhelm defenders around the basket. His powerful frame, 6'10" wingspan and vertical pop make him dangerous in transition, as a cutter and attacking closeouts. Developing a more reliable jumper and polished creation game will be important, but his physical tools give him significant two-way upside.

9.name: Kellen Thornton
9.about: One of the most versatile frontcourt prospects in the class, Thornton has played his way into the top-10 conversation during his freshman season at UCLA. He combines explosive rim finishing and disruptive interior defense with legitimate shooting touch from the perimeter, giving him the tools to impact games in multiple ways. His two-way versatility gives him considerable upside as a modern NBA big.

10.name: Gero Brecht
10.about: An enticing combination of size, length and explosive athleticism has pushed Brecht into the top-10 conversation among international prospects. He attacks open lanes aggressively, finishes above the rim and uses his 7'2" wingspan to make plays defensively against professional competition. His perimeter skill remains a work in progress, but his physical tools provide an exciting foundation for long-term development.

11.name: Tai Scott
11.about: A polished pull-up scorer, Scott entered the season with top-10 expectations before seeing his stock slip just outside that range. His shot-making remained impressive, particularly stopping behind screens and creating from the midrange, but questions about his size, defensive limitations and finishing against length became more prominent. His scoring craft and playmaking still give him a strong lottery-level offensive profile.

12.name: Evan Williams
12.about: Widely regarded as the best defender in the class, Williams established himself as an elite defensive prospect immediately at Villanova. His 6'11" wingspan, strength, quickness and instincts allow him to suffocate opposing guards, disrupt passing lanes and comfortably switch onto bigger players. He also flashes downhill creation and playmaking offensively, but his inconsistent jumper remains the primary obstacle to becoming a high-level two-way guard.

13.name: Kylian Terry Jr.
13.about: A polished senior guard and one of the class's more dangerous perimeter scorers, Terry built his first-round case around high-level shooting and experienced guard play. He can bury threes off the catch or dribble, manipulate screens and punish defenders who go underneath. His age and average athleticism limit some of the upside, but his shooting gives him a clear NBA-ready skill.

14.name: Kévin N’Goma
14.about: N’Goma has emerged as one of the more appealing two-way forwards in the class, earning mid-first-round consideration with his defense and improving perimeter skill. His 7'1" wingspan allows him to disrupt wings, switch across multiple positions and generate deflections, while his shooting provides a clean offensive fit. He projects as a highly adaptable complementary piece with room to expand his game.

15.name: Jokūbas Kanapinskas
15.about: After entering the season as a preseason top-five prospect, Kanapinskas saw his stock slide into the middle of the first round despite flashing an unusual offensive skill set at 6'8". His size, passing vision and perimeter shooting remain highly intriguing, but concerns about his burst, rim pressure and defensive limitations became more pronounced. The upside remains, though his freshman season exposed areas that require further development.

16.name: Noé Bellanger
16.about: Legitimate guard skills in a 6'9" frame have made Bellanger one of the class's more intriguing oversized creators. Against professional competition in France, he has shown the ability to initiate offense, manipulate defenses as a passer and knock down shots from the perimeter. His average athleticism limits some of his scoring upside, but his combination of size, shooting and playmaking gives him considerable lineup versatility.

17.name: Damir Thompson
17.about: Once viewed as a likely top-10 pick, Thompson slipped into the mid-first-round range after an uneven sophomore season at Arizona State. His 6'7" frame still gives him intriguing versatility as a combo guard, allowing him to create for teammates, score over smaller defenders and operate on or off the ball. The talent remains evident, but greater consistency as a creator would help him recapture some of his earlier draft momentum.

18.name: Will Jennings Jr.
18.about: Jennings emerged as one of the class's more intriguing developmental guards, with his freshman season offering flashes of what he could eventually become rather than a finished product. His 6'9" wingspan, downhill creativity and scoring flashes give him an exciting foundation, while his jumper has shown encouraging potential. He remains inconsistent as a decision-maker and creator, but continued development could unlock considerably more offensive upside.

19.name: Isaiah Washington
19.about: A former five-star recruit, Washington showed why he was so highly regarded with flashes of high-level two-way potential during his freshman season at Kentucky. His powerful 212-pound frame, 6'9" wingspan and downhill aggression allow him to bully his way into the paint and finish through contact. His jumper and decision-making remain inconsistent, but the physical foundation gives him significant developmental upside.

20.name: Derrick Starks
20.about: A throwback interior presence with legitimate NBA size, Starks made an immediate impact at Michigan State through physicality, rebounding and low-post scoring. He establishes deep position, finishes through contact and consistently creates second-chance opportunities on the glass. His combination of strength, length and interior production gives him first-round appeal despite a game largely confined to the paint.

21.name: Caleb Hankins
21.about: Hankins has developed into an intriguing first-round prospect by combining disruptive frontcourt defense with unusual open-floor ability. The UConn sophomore protects the rim with his 7'3" wingspan, cleans the glass and can immediately push the ball himself to ignite transition opportunities. His developing jumper and half-court offense remain swing skills, but his defensive versatility gives him a clear NBA foundation.

22.name: Jirani Robinson
22.about: A breakout junior season at Missouri established Robinson as a legitimate three-level scorer and elevated his draft stock. He can punish defenses from deep, create pull-ups in the midrange and use his strength to finish when attacking closeouts. His scoring versatility gives him a strong offensive foundation, though improving his playmaking and defensive consistency will determine how large a role he can handle at the next level.

23.name: Justin Reese
23.about: After spending his first two seasons at Michigan, Reese transferred to Villanova and developed into a polished perimeter scorer over his final two years. He excels creating pull-ups, changing pace to generate separation and scoring comfortably from multiple levels. His extensive college experience gives him one of the more refined offensive games in the class, although modest physical tools limit his long-term ceiling.

24.name: Cornelius Jefferson II
24.about: Jefferson has overcome unconventional size for a frontcourt prospect by playing with tremendous strength, length and physicality around the basket. The Oregon freshman uses his 7'0" wingspan to battle bigger players on the glass, finishes forcefully through contact and brings consistent energy defensively. His production and physical tools have pushed him into the late-first-round conversation despite questions about his offensive fit.

25.name: Marquise Tyler
25.about: One of the better defensive wings in the freshman class, Tyler used his length, athleticism and motor to take on difficult assignments for USC. He can pressure ball handlers, switch across multiple positions and create transition opportunities with his defense. His offensive game remains fairly limited, but continued shooting development could make him a valuable two-way role player.

26.name: Bronte Johnson
26.about: Explosive athleticism gives Johnson one of the more intriguing developmental profiles among the guards in this class. His powerful 218-pound frame, burst and vertical pop make him extremely difficult to contain once he gets downhill, allowing him to finish through or above contact. His jumper and half-court command remain raw, but his physical tools provide substantial upside if his guard skills continue developing.

27.name: Levi Jones
27.about: After transferring from Syracuse to Alabama, Jones took on a larger role and developed into a productive on-ball creator during his sophomore season. The 6'5" guard plays with patience, using changes of pace, footwork and a polished midrange game to manufacture offense while creating for teammates. His size and feel are appealing, though inconsistent perimeter shooting and average athleticism remain concerns.

28.name: Mathys Moreau
28.about: Already earning minutes against professional competition in France, Moreau has established himself as an intriguing late-first-round big. He provides a clear vertical threat as a rim runner, uses his length effectively around the basket and shows promising mobility defensively. Flashes of touch away from the rim add another layer to his developmental upside.

29.name: Mike Rooney
29.about: A skilled offensive guard with a strong blend of shooting and playmaking, Rooney emerged as California's primary initiator during his junior season. The lefty operates comfortably out of ball screens, can punish defenders who go under with his jumper and consistently creates opportunities for teammates. His average athleticism and limited rim pressure lower his ceiling, but his offensive feel gives him a clear pathway as a backup point guard.

30.name: NaQuian Smith Jr.
30.about: A former top-10 recruit, Smith transferred from Oregon to Minnesota looking for a larger opportunity and began translating his considerable talent into more consistent production. The strong, long-armed guard can create pull-ups, overpower smaller defenders and generate offense off the bounce. His efficiency and decision-making still fluctuate, but his pedigree and physical tools leave room for further development.

31.name: T.J. Anderson
31.about: One of the better perimeter shooters in the class, Anderson built his draft case around a highly productive senior season at Wichita State. He is dangerous spotting up, relocating without the ball and pulling up when defenders give him space, with enough size to shoot over smaller guards. Limited athleticism restricts his rim pressure and defensive versatility, but his shooting gives him a clear NBA role.

32.name: Jake Jewell
32.about: A seasoned anchor in the middle for UConn, Jewell enters the draft with a well-defined interior role. He uses his 263-pound frame to establish position, score with patient post moves and hold his ground defensively, while providing serviceable rim protection. His experience and physicality make him a potential early-second-round option for teams seeking traditional center depth.

33.name: Aquintis Sims
33.about: Defensive activity has become Sims' legitimate NBA calling card at Temple, where his length, strength and quick reactions consistently disrupt passing lanes and create turnovers. He is particularly dangerous once those stops become transition opportunities, where his athleticism shines. His half-court offense remains relatively basic, but his defensive playmaking gives him a clear second-round pathway.

34.name: TreKell Perry
34.about: Built like a defensive specialist at 223 pounds, Perry has emerged as one of the more physically imposing perimeter defenders in the class. He uses strength, length and athleticism to pressure guards, absorb contact against wings and switch across multiple positions. His offensive skill set remains fairly limited, but improved shooting has given him enough complementary value to warrant early-second-round consideration.

35.name: Tre Lang
35.about: After making one stop at Penn State and another at Arizona, Lang finally found stability at UCLA, where he settled into a major playmaking role during his junior season. The pass-first guard excels at getting into the paint, keeping his dribble alive and finding teammates once defenses collapse. His scoring ceiling remains modest, but his vision and ability to organize an offense give him a viable backup point-guard pathway.

36.name: Brandyn Stephens
36.about: Stephens built a productive senior season around movement, energy and efficient finishing rather than needing touches called for him. He consistently finds openings as a cutter, crashes the offensive glass and provides an active target around the rim. His limited perimeter game caps some of his versatility, but his ability to contribute without the ball gives him a viable second-round role-player profile.

37.name: Ty Davis
37.about: An explosive scoring guard despite his smaller frame, Davis flashed intriguing offensive upside throughout his freshman season at Arkansas. He attacks openings aggressively, plays above his size around the basket and has shown encouraging touch from beyond the arc. His combination of scoring pop and youth makes him an appealing developmental prospect, though size and playmaking questions complicate his projection as a full-time point guard.

38.name: Yves Maréchal
38.about: A useful role against high-level professional competition with Monaco has helped Maréchal earn second-round consideration. The lefty attacks gaps decisively, cuts well behind defenses and has enough shooting touch to keep defenders honest away from the basket. He lacks a standout creation skill, but his size, finishing and complementary offensive game give him an appealing role-player profile.

39.name: Ronnie Freeman
39.about: Defense and reliability have become Freeman's calling cards after four seasons at Florida. His 6'7" wingspan allows him to pressure opposing guards, disrupt passing lanes and defend beyond his listed size, while his spot-up jumper provides value away from the ball. He is not a dynamic lead creator, but his defense, experience and low-maintenance offensive game give him a clear role-player pathway.

40.name: Mikey Ng'anamu
40.about: An aggressive downhill attacker, Ng'anamu made his mark at Iowa State with his ability to explode into open lanes and finish above the rim. The lefty uses his 6'9" wingspan and athleticism to play bigger than his 6'4" frame, particularly in transition and as a cutter. His perimeter shooting and half-court creation remain inconsistent, but his slashing ability gives him an intriguing developmental foundation.

41.name: Jeremiah Herrington
41.about: Intriguing scoring flashes highlighted Herrington's freshman season at Arizona, particularly when creating jumpers from the midrange and attacking defenders off one or two dribbles. His 6'11" wingspan gives him useful defensive tools and helps compensate for average athleticism. Becoming a more consistent three-point shooter and decision-maker will be key to turning those flashes into a dependable NBA role.

42.name: Daniel Rivas
42.about: A big, attacking guard with legitimate playmaking ability, Rivas has earned draft consideration while competing professionally with Baskonia. He uses his 6'6" frame to get downhill, finish through contact and draw extra defenders before finding teammates on the move. His combination of slashing, passing and developing perimeter shooting gives him intriguing offensive versatility, though greater scoring consistency would strengthen his NBA projection.

43.name: Tristin Stanton
43.about: A polished isolation scorer with legitimate shooting range, Stanton became VCU's primary perimeter weapon during his junior season. He creates space with footwork and changes of pace, can punish defenders from deep and competes defensively despite limited athleticism. His lack of burst makes separation more difficult against higher-level defenders, but his shot-making gives him a viable second-round pathway.

44.name: Brodie Matthews
44.about: Touch and creativity inside the arc have helped Matthews develop into an intriguing second-round prospect. He is comfortable attacking mismatches, getting to short pull-ups and using scoop finishes and floaters around length. His perimeter shooting remains inconsistent, but his scoring touch and experience against professional competition provide an interesting offensive foundation.

45.name: Julian Hayward
45.about: Hayward developed into a productive interior role player during his sophomore season at Oklahoma, generating much of his offense through cutting, offensive rebounds and opportunistic finishes. His length and sturdy frame allow him to compete effectively on the glass despite being undersized for a traditional center. He projects as a second-round developmental big whose value will come primarily without the ball.

46.name: Miles Baker
46.about: Baker turned a featured role at San Francisco into legitimate draft consideration, showcasing uncommon shot-making ability for a forward his size. He is comfortable attacking off the dribble, getting to pull-ups and using his length to shoot over smaller defenders. His scoring versatility makes him an intriguing second-round option, though proving he can contribute consistently without the ball will be important at the next level.

47.name: Drew Phillips
47.about: After spending his first three seasons at Oklahoma, Phillips transferred to UConn for his senior year and established himself as a dependable perimeter weapon. He excels working around screens, relocating into open space and creating quick pull-ups from beyond the arc. His shooting and extensive college experience give him a defined offensive role, though limited size and athleticism raise questions about his defensive translation.

48.name: Caspian Williams
48.about: A well-rounded game and knack for finding productive ways to score inside the arc have pushed Williams into the second-round picture. He uses footwork, strength and touch to finish around defenders while providing dependable defense across multiple forward matchups. He lacks a defining high-end skill, but his versatility and professional experience give him a chance to compete for a rotation role.

49.name: Isaiah Ennis
49.about: Two translatable skills give Ennis a straightforward NBA case: perimeter shooting and defense. The Baylor freshman spaces the floor efficiently off the catch and uses his 6'11" wingspan, positioning and anticipation to bother opposing wings despite limited athleticism. He offers little creation off the dribble, but his ability to contribute without needing touches gives him a clear role-player pathway.

50.name: Daran Jenkins
50.about: Jenkins turned his senior year at DePaul into a strong showcase of his energy and defensive versatility. His 7'3" wingspan and athleticism allow him to protect the rim, switch onto different matchups and play above the basket, while an improving jumper gives him some stretch potential. He profiles as an experienced second-round option with a pathway toward becoming a useful defensive role player.

51.name: Max Stanley Jr
51.about: Stanley has played himself into the second-round picture by offering an appealing mix of shooting, passing and defensive versatility at Montana. He can space the floor, make quick reads when defenses rotate and use his strength and length against multiple positions. His lack of traditional power-forward size creates matchup questions, but his complementary skill set gives him a pathway toward an NBA role.

52.name: Jonathan Parrish
52.about: Physical tools drive Parrish's appeal after an uneven but promising freshman season at Houston. His powerful 213-pound frame, 6'9" wingspan and vertical ability make him dangerous attacking the basket and give him intriguing defensive potential. His guard skills are still developing, particularly as a shooter and decision-maker, but his youth and physical profile make him an interesting second-round project.

53.name: Aji Mwanjerugo
53.about: By thriving as a cutter, transition runner and opportunistic finisher, Mwanjerugo carved out a valuable role during his senior season at Kansas. His length allows him to finish creatively around the basket and contribute defensively across the wing, while he rarely needs designed touches to make an impact. His limited creation and inconsistent jumper cap his offensive ceiling, leaving him as a potential energy wing at the next level.

54.name: Ben Bagwell
54.about: A polished veteran with four years of college experience, Bagwell built his NBA case around skill rather than athleticism. He can punish mismatches on the block, step outside for catch-and-shoot threes and use his strength to create space inside. At 24, his projection is largely tied to whether his shooting and interior scoring can translate into a dependable reserve role.

55.name: Endre Baranyai
55.about: Baranyai has drawn second-round interest with an unusual offensive skill set for a frontcourt player, showing touch as a passer and scorer against professional competition in Hungary. He operates comfortably from the elbows and mid-post, where he can find cutters or create turnaround jumpers. His offensive feel is intriguing, though limited athleticism and defensive versatility cloud his NBA projection.

56.name: Wilhelm Sundberg
56.about: A productive interior presence in Sweden, Sundberg has built his game around strength, touch and methodical scoring from the mid-post. The lefty uses positioning and footwork to create favorable looks while providing dependable work on the glass. His limited mobility lowers his defensive ceiling, making him a late-second-round prospect whose offensive skill will need to drive his NBA value.

57.name: Brennon McBride
57.about: A confident left-handed shot-maker, McBride developed into a dangerous perimeter weapon during his sophomore season at Marquette. He can connect from deep off the catch, relocate into open windows and create pull-ups when defenders give him space. His shooting provides a clear offensive skill, but limited burst and playmaking leave questions about how much he can offer when his jumper is not falling.

58.name: Jaden Quinn
58.about: A former five-star recruit, Quinn spent his first two college seasons at LSU before transferring to Duke for his junior year. He has settled into a physical interior role built around rebounding, toughness and defensive effort, using his strong frame and 7'2" wingspan effectively around the basket. His pedigree remains intriguing, but limited offensive development has pushed him toward the late-second-round range.

59.name: Bryan Boyce
59.about: Reliable shooting and two-way activity have kept Boyce on the draft radar following his junior season at Gonzaga. Still only 20, he is notably young for his class, leaving more developmental runway than the typical three-year college prospect. He contributes as a spot-up shooter, relocates well around the arc and competes defensively, giving him a potential developmental 3-and-D pathway.

60.name: Konstantinos Apostolakis
60.about: Apostolakis has worked his way onto the draft radar as a developmental frontcourt prospect with appealing length and finishing tools. He uses his 7'3" wingspan effectively as a cutter, lob target and help defender while competing against professionals in Greece. His offensive game remains limited outside the paint, making his long-term value heavily dependent on defense and finishing.

61.name: Jay Tucker
61.about: A polished combination of shooting and secondary playmaking at 6'7" has put Tucker on the fringe of the draft conversation. He can knock down threes off the catch or dribble, attack aggressive closeouts and keep the offense moving with quick reads. His lack of athleticism creates concerns defensively and around the rim, but his size and offensive skill give him a potential specialist role.

62.name: Jasen Howard
62.about: Howard has emerged as a fringe draft prospect by providing Villanova with a mobile floor-spacing option in the frontcourt. He moves well without the ball, can stretch defenses with his catch-and-shoot ability and has enough mobility to attack closeouts when given space. Developing more physicality and defensive consistency will be important for him to secure an NBA role.

63.name: Rasheed Williams
63.about: Energy and defensive versatility have defined Williams' senior season at Tennessee, where he has consistently taken on difficult perimeter assignments. His 6'10" wingspan and athleticism allow him to pressure ball handlers, generate turnovers and turn stops into transition opportunities. His offensive skill set remains limited, but his defense and open-floor ability give him a pathway as an end-of-rotation two-way guard.

64.name: Anrijs Celmiņš
64.about: A scoring-minded wing with good size, Celmiņš has played his way onto the draft fringe through his production against professional competition in Latvia. He hunts scoring opportunities from multiple levels but is also a capable secondary playmaker, using his size to see passing windows and create for teammates when defenses collapse. His scoring instincts remain his calling card, though defensive consistency and shot selection need improvement.

65.name: Tyrice Henderson
65.about: A skilled offensive point guard, Henderson carved out a productive role at Pittsburgh with his combination of perimeter shooting and playmaking. He operates comfortably out of ball screens, can create pull-up threes when defenders go under and keeps teammates involved as a facilitator. His lack of size and athleticism limits his margin for error, leaving him as a fringe-draft prospect despite his offensive skill.

66.name: Jorden Olivarez
66.about: Olivarez has generated fringe draft interest with a skill-heavy offensive game built around shooting and passing. He stretches defenses well beyond the arc and makes intelligent reads from the perimeter, giving Louisville another facilitator in the frontcourt. His lack of athleticism and unconventional size for a big create significant defensive questions, but his offensive versatility offers a potential specialist pathway.

67.name: Alim Bayraktaroğlu
67.about: Bayraktaroğlu has earned draft consideration through his touch and polished interior skill against professional competition in Türkiye. He operates comfortably from the mid-post, using patient footwork, fakes and soft finishes rather than overwhelming defenders physically. With limited shooting range and modest defensive tools, he projects as a fringe draft prospect competing for a developmental backup-center role.

68.name: Jaleel Shelby
68.about: A productive veteran guard, Shelby built his draft case around polished creation inside the arc and the ability to control possessions with the ball in his hands. He uses changes of pace, strength and footwork to reach his spots while providing capable secondary playmaking. At 24, his limited developmental runway works against him, but his experience and scoring craft could translate to a backup-guard role.

69.name: Dillan Keefer
69.about: Keefer put together a productive senior season at Notre Dame by embracing a physical, low-maintenance role in the frontcourt. He creates extra possessions on the glass, sets hard screens and does most of his scoring through cuts, rolls and finishes around the basket. His limited perimeter skill and average athleticism restrict his ceiling, but his toughness gives him a potential depth-big pathway.

70.name: Maynard Jones Jr.
70.about: A productive senior scorer at Hofstra, Jones built his game around attacking downhill, finishing through traffic and finding opportunities above the rim. His 6'10" wingspan helps him play bigger than his listed height on both ends, while an improved jumper gives him some complementary value away from the basket. His limited creation and playmaking keep him in fringe-draft territory.

71.name: Samson Farrington
71.about: Toughness, physicality and reliable perimeter shooting formed the foundation of Farrington's draft case at Pepperdine. The 23-year-old senior competes on both ends, battles bigger forwards and consistently provides spacing as a catch-and-shoot threat. His age and limited creation leave little room for projection, but his shooting and willingness to handle physical assignments could earn him an opportunity as a depth wing.

72.name: Mac Flynn
72.about: An aggressive slashing guard, Flynn made his mark at UCLA by attacking gaps, pushing the pace and playing much bigger than his 6'0" frame around the basket. His left-handed drives and willingness to challenge defenders create occasional explosive finishes, but his lack of size and reliable perimeter shooting significantly complicate his NBA projection. He profiles as a fringe-draft guard who will need to earn opportunities through energy and rim pressure.

73.name: Julien Richey
73.about: An ability to manufacture perimeter offense for Tennessee has put Richey on the fringe of the draft conversation. He is comfortable working into pull-ups, using screens to find shooting windows and attacking defenders who close out too aggressively. His lack of ideal size and athleticism for an NBA wing creates concerns, while inconsistent efficiency prevents his shot-making from becoming a true standout skill.

74.name: Johnnie Matthews
74.about: A veteran perimeter specialist, Matthews carved out a valuable offensive role at Gonzaga with his ability to stretch defenses well beyond the arc. He is comfortable firing off the catch, relocating for open looks and using screens to create shooting windows. His lack of athleticism and limited length create concerns defensively, making his shooting efficiency critical to his chances of sticking at the next level.

75.name: Braden Lowe
75.about: Lowe enters the draft as an experienced stretch big whose shooting gives him a chance to compete for an NBA opportunity. He spaces effectively as a pick-and-pop threat, understands how to relocate around the perimeter and plays within his role offensively. At 23 with limited length and athleticism, however, his defensive limitations leave him firmly on the draft fringe.
